other_side: Where NLW treats the extinction debate as unfalsifiable but worth having loudly, Zitron's manifesto of a fortnight earlier treats the whole premise as a category error. Talk of 'recursive self-improvement' is, in his words, 'ridiculous', an industry too lazy to explain how a model would train itself; and doomers warning of superintelligence have enjoyed enormous media prominence without stopping a single thing or substantiating a single concern. He argues the real danger is already here and mundane: labs letting unreliable software loose in unsafe network environments with near-unlimited resources, driven by revenue targets and the need to justify hundreds of billions in capex. In his telling the doom story and the hype story are the same product, sold by people who need you to believe the models are far more powerful than they are.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether today's models are on a path to something qualitatively more capable, or an expensive plateau dressed up as a trajectory. Both accept as fact that the viral posts said nothing new, that lab incentives shape every message, and that the concrete harms worth attention now are cyber and agentic misbehaviour, with the Hugging Face breach as the shared example. The empirical question that will resolve is whether capability keeps compounding as training spend rises; the observable is whether the next frontier generation, arriving after 2027's capex bills fall due, is measurably better at real tasks rather than benchmarks. The worldview residue is whether a low-probability catastrophe deserves policy before evidence. NLW is vindicated if capability keeps jumping and the debate yields specific oversight rather than bans; Zitron if progress stalls and doom talk fades with the funding. Both are polemicists with incentives, one bullish and anti-doom, the other bubble-certain and anti-hype; the signal is their shared insistence that present, specific harms deserve the attention. Watch whether any lab publishes a concrete pacing proposal.
